name: Ben Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. This is confidential. What does your usual workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Ben Olsen, 43, and I am a junior hand doing formwork and general carpentry on a hotel building site. I left school before finishing and still need the lead carpenter to check my set-out before a pour. Saturdays bring in a higher wage than most site jobs, though I miss some of my children’s games. I have never used an AI tool; a level and a patient teacher are what I use each day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the situation at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner has a regular pharmacy job, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We saved about twelve months of living costs by working long shifts and keeping big purchases back. There are plenty of builders nearby, but a new crew would have to learn what I can and cannot do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the men on the hotel build that a machine can sort the order sheets, but the formwork still has to sit square. I have never used an AI tool and do not need one to carry a level. Give me a clear drawing and a patient carpenter instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43 and still junior at this trade, though the Saturday shifts pay better than most site jobs. My partner's pharmacy wage is regular, and we have a year's living costs saved against our mortgage. A slow bit of software would not change my place on the concrete crew much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid formwork shifts and ask the lead carpenter to check my first corner each morning. In the first year I would keep paying an extra amount against the mortgage after each Saturday shift. I would also keep taking the marked-up drawing home to study the next day's pour, as long as the site allows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I worry more about a wet board slipping under my boots than about an office program. Our two children have school expenses, but we planned for those before anybody mentioned AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the first corner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I set one corner half a finger out last month and the lead carpenter caught it before the crew poured. We had to move the timber, which was humbling. A quiet check at the start is better than breaking concrete later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do Saturdays mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner covers the children’s matches and I go when I can. The extra wage has built our savings and kept the loan balance moving down. I would like to be home more once we owe less.

I would ask for a **clear drawing** and patient carpentry checks.
think: I am a **junior** worker despite higher Saturday pay.
Our **year of savings** and regular second wage protect the mortgage.

Pay extra toward the **mortgage** after Saturday shifts.
feel: **Calm** about work, with ordinary attention to site hazards.
S0.quote: A quiet check at the start is better than breaking concrete later.
fieldNote: Ben uses a real **crooked-corner mistake** to explain his preference for a skilled person over software.
The family has **twelve months saved**, making his main present sacrifice Saturday time with the children.

steps.text: Keep paid hotel formwork shifts and request first-corner checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may buy timber and book deliveries faster, which could help us finish a pour on time. I would still ask who checks the order against the drawing. If management wants fewer hands because a list is faster, I would expect them to say so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel build will still need people to set forms, but smoother schedules might mean fewer Saturday shifts. That is where my higher pay comes from. We could cover the mortgage without the premium for a while, but we would lose the room to pay it down early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the formwork crew and ask the site manager each Friday what Saturday work is actually booked. If the premium shifts fall for two months, I would call three nearby builders about their weekend rates. In the first year I would stop counting overtime in the family budget and keep teaching myself set-out from the carpenter's drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not desperate. I can work another site, but I would have to prove myself to a new lead carpenter. I would not chase a new program just to look busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner if overtime fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the children keep their lessons, while we slow the extra mortgage payments. My partner knows the basic wages cover regular bills. We would wait for actual payslips before cancelling anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the new ordering program?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is not my task on this site. If it becomes part of formwork, I would need someone to show me a proven way to use it safely. Right now I need to set corners better and keep a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office and design work change by 2028, and capable robots reach our formwork around 2031. The contractor should explain what happens to the crew before buying equipment. A builder can buy a machine, but it still owes workers honest notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 when robots can do the hands-on part. A year's savings can carry the mortgage through a gap, not through the rest of my working life. There are plenty of sites here now, but their owners might all make the same choice by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid shift and ask the site manager for the booked jobs beyond this hotel. This winter I would speak to two small renovation builders about paid openings, because I have done patching on old forms. In the first year after 2028 I would apply if either has a real place and put Saturday pay toward the mortgage instead of our planned garden room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes me anxious. I am slow to change and I know it, but I can still make calls. I would hate to tell my children we waited until the savings were gone before looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why renovation work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old walls make each form a little different, and I have helped patch a few. I cannot promise robots will never handle it. I would go where somebody is paying me now and keep my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them the garden room is waiting and their school costs are not the reason. My partner and I handle the loan, not the children. A year of savings gives us time to do that without frightening them every evening.

say: I would tell the crew **2028 thinking AI** comes before 2031 site robots.
I would ask the contractor for **honest notice** about jobs.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots could do formwork.
A year of savings cannot replace a **working lifetime** if builders all automate.
do: Keep every paid **hotel shift** and ask about the next booked job.
Apply to **two renovation builders** if they offer real paid places.
Pay Saturday earnings against the **mortgage** instead of building a garden room.
feel: **Anxious** about the short window and his own slow pace of change.
S2.quote: A year's savings can carry the mortgage through a gap, not through the rest of my working life.
fieldNote: Ben treats the **one-year reserve** as time to search, not an income substitute.
His renovation idea offers **paid work now**, while he acknowledges capable robots may eventually manage old walls too.

steps.text: Keep every paid hotel shift and ask about booked work beyond the site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and site robots reach formwork about 2034. Five years lets an honest contractor show the crew its plans well ahead of the first machine. I would ask for a written list of likely shifts, not a pep talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the thinking date and 51 at the robot date. Our children will be older, but the mortgage may not be gone. Five years could let us cut the balance down and let me become a better carpenter before I have to look for a different site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid Saturday work and ask the lead carpenter for one harder set-out task a month, with him checking it. My partner and I would put the premium toward the mortgage every quarter. In the first year after 2031 I would call nearby builders about paid work if the hotel contractor cuts shifts and stay employed until there is an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less anxious than with two years. I do not enjoy planning for machines I cannot see yet. The five-year warning at least gives me time to do the work in front of me well and lower the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a harder task be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set the curve for a stair landing instead of only carrying boards, while the carpenter checks my marks. If I make a bad mark, I want to learn why before the pour. A skill I can show another builder is worth more than saying I worked hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a course with no job attached. If a builder offered a paid apprenticeship in a trade they still need, I would look at it with my partner. I left school early and learn best with tools and a patient teacher.

say: I would ask for a **written shift plan** before 2034 site robots arrive.
I would tell coworkers five years allows real **carpentry practice**.
think: I would be **51** when robots can do formwork, with a possible mortgage.
A smaller **loan balance** would give my family more room.
do: Keep **Saturday shifts** and practice harder set-out tasks under supervision.

S3.quote: A skill I can show another builder is worth more than saying I worked hard.
fieldNote: Ben values **supervised craft practice** and an actual wage offer more than a vague course.

steps.text: Keep paid Saturday shifts and practice harder set-out with the carpenter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office changes by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade is time enough to work, save and teach younger hands while the trade still needs us. I would want builders to show what their machines do before telling families to change plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 at the robot date. Our children will be grown, so school costs should no longer take the same share. If the Saturday work holds, the mortgage could be cleared, but I cannot assume I can retire at 56 just because the loan is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on paid formwork shifts and ask the carpenter to teach me the landing work properly. We would review the mortgage each year and use the premiums for extra payments while keeping our savings intact. In the first year after 2036 I would ask for the contractor's actual site robot plan and ring other builders if the roster begins to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. It is easier to work steadily with a long warning than to gamble on a machine story. I would still want a wage after 2039, even if the mortgage is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a younger worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to sight along a form and ask for a second check before the pour. I am junior myself, so I would pass on only what I can actually do. A patient apprenticeship is how the trade survives mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mortgage is cleared early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep some of the Saturday money aside and I might take fewer shifts to see the family. I would not call the savings a pension. My partner and I still need ordinary income after the loan ends.

I would defend patient **apprenticeships** for younger workers.

fieldNote: He imagines grown children and a possible cleared **mortgage**, while explicitly rejecting an assumed retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our hands-on work faces capable robots around 2031. Clear notice of site jobs, an honest chance to learn with a carpenter and paid openings at nearby builders would help. I can use savings during a gap, but I want to keep earning for my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the new hands while the old work still exists. I am still learning at 43, and a patient carpenter has saved more timber than any poster about new skills. Apprenticeships need paid days on a real site.

headlineQuote: I am still learning at 43, and a patient carpenter has saved more timber than any poster about new skills.
portrait: Ben is a **43-year-old junior** formwork worker on a hotel site, learning from a lead carpenter after leaving school early.
Saturday shifts bring **higher pay**, while his partner’s pharmacy wage and twelve months saved support two children and a mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and prefers marked drawings, a level and supervised practice.
As robot deadlines shorten, he seeks **paid building work**, mortgage relief and honest notice rather than trusting an untested course.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives his hands-on formwork only until around 2031 before capable robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **job notice**, supervised carpentry practice and real paid openings at nearby builders would preserve income.
